html:
Powhatan was the name of an Algonquian-speaking people of Tidewater Virginia, and of the paramount chiefdom they led when the English arrived in 1607. Its homeland, which its people called Tsenacommacah, lay along the James, York and Rappahannock rivers around Chesapeake Bay.

Its great chief, Wahunsenacawh, was known to the English simply as Powhatan. He inherited about six tribes in the late 1500s and, through war and marriage, built a chiefdom of about thirty, among them the Appomattoc, Chickahominy, Mattaponi, Nansemond and Rappahannock. Each tribe had its own weroance (chief) and paid tribute in corn, skins and copper to him. People lived in villages of bark houses, grew maize, beans and squash, fished and hunted.

The English colony of Jamestown was built inside this land in 1607. John Smith, who explored and mapped the region in 1608, recorded many of its towns. Trade and kidnapping, marriage and war followed: Powhatan's daughter Pocahontas married the colonist John Rolfe in 1614. Under his brother Opechancanough the Powhatan struck the colony in 1622 and 1644, but the growth of the tobacco plantations pushed them off their lands. By the treaties of 1646 and 1677 the surviving tribes became tributaries of Virginia. Several, such as the Pamunkey and Mattaponi, still hold small reservations.
